Verify Now Blog > Extrude: Check Your 3D Models on Your Phone Before Printing Extrude: Check Your 3D Models on Your Phone Before Printing by: Mila Nov 19,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Before starting a 3D print, it's worth checking your model's dimensions, structure, and printability. But what if you could do all of this directly on your phone? Meet Extrude, a free 3D model viewer app for iPhone, iPad, and Android, designed to help makers inspect their 3D models anytime, anywhere. What Is Extrude? Extrude supports a wide range of 3D file formats, including STL, 3MF, OBJ, PLY, GLB, and G-code. You can open files directly on your phone, even offline, without creating an account or uploading anything. Your files stay on your device. Extrude also includes several tools to help you prepare your models for printing: View & Measure: View 3D models and measure their dimensions. Print Check: Check printer bed fit and wall thickness. Print Estimates: Estimate printing time and filament usage. Section View: Inspect the internal structure of 3D models. AR Preview: View models at actual size in your surroundings. Available in 27 languages, Extrude is continuing to grow its user community among makers worldwide. Extrude x PCBWay: From Digital Models to Physical Parts Not every project can be completed with a desktop 3D printer. Sometimes you need a larger part, different materials, or more precise manufacturing. That's where PCBWay comes in! Starting November 23, 2026, Extrude users will see a PCBWay banner directly in the 3D viewer. Through this collaboration, users can discover PCBWay's professional manufacturing services, including 3D printing and CNC machining, with over 100 material options! Try Extrude Today! Want to inspect your 3D models more conveniently? Give Extrude a try! Extrude website: https://getextrude.com/ STL viewer: https://getextrude.com/stl-viewer/ Get it on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.sakasstudio.stlview Download on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/us/app/stl-viewer-3d-model-3mf/id6801906359 Learn More about How to Open STL Files on Your Phone: https://getextrude.com/blog/open-stl-files-on-iphone/ https://getextrude.com/blog/open-stl-files-on-android/ Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement 12 PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Component Placement by: Mila Oct 29,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB Layout PCB Component Placement PCB Layout Guidelines PCB Design Guidelines PCB layout involves more than simply placing components and routing traces. Component spacing, decoupling capacitor placement, pad connections, thermal management, and manufacturing constraints all affect PCB assembly quality and long-term reliability. The following PCB layout guidelines cover 12 practical details that engineers should consider during PCB component placement and design. 1. SMT Component Spacing The spacing between surface-mount technology (SMT) components is an important consideration in PCB layout. Insufficient spacing can make solder paste printing and component placement more difficult, increase the risk of solder bridging, and complicate rework and maintenance. The following values can serve as preliminary references for PCB component spacing: Same-type components: A spacing of at least 0.3 mm may be used as a reference. Different types of components: A spacing of at least 0.13 × h + 0.3 mm may be used as a reference, where h is the maximum height difference between adjacent components. Components requiring manual placement or rework: A spacing of at least 1.5 mm may be considered, depending on the available working space and tools. These values are for reference only and are not universal manufacturing standards. Actual PCB component spacing should be determined based on component packages, pad dimensions, solder paste printing, placement equipment, and the manufacturing and assembly capabilities of the PCB supplier. 2. Spacing Between Through-Hole and SMT Components Adequate spacing should also be maintained between through-hole components and SMT components to prevent interference during component placement, soldering, and subsequent rework. A spacing of 1–3 mm can serve as a general reference, but the actual distance depends on component dimensions, lead positions, soldering methods, and maintenance requirements. For PCBs assembled using wave soldering, engineers should also consider component orientation, shadowing effects caused by adjacent components, and whether solder can reach the joints effectively. 3. IC Decoupling Capacitor Placement Decoupling capacitors should be placed as close as practical to the corresponding IC power pins. This helps shorten the current loop between the power supply and ground, reducing parasitic inductance and power supply noise. When an IC has multiple power pins, the number, capacitance, and placement of decoupling capacitors should be determined according to the datasheet, power distribution network, and actual current requirements. Where individual power pins require dedicated decoupling, the corresponding capacitors should be placed as close to those pins as possible. The grounding path is equally important. Keep the connections between the power pin, decoupling capacitor, and ground as short as practical. Unnecessarily long traces or excessive vias can reduce decoupling effectiveness, particularly at high frequencies. 4. Component Orientation and Clearance Near PCB Edges PCBs often undergo routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes. Components near PCB edges therefore require special attention to their orientation and clearance. First, consider the mechanical stress generated during depanelization. Ceramic capacitors, connectors, and other mechanically sensitive components should be positioned to minimize stress concentration at solder joints and component bodies. Component orientation should be determined by the depanelization method, pad geometry, and component characteristics rather than by a universal rule that all components must be parallel to the cutting direction. Second, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near PCB edges to prevent damage from cutting tools or depanelization equipment. The required clearance depends on the depanelization method, such as V-scoring, routing, or mouse bites, as well as component dimensions and the PCB manufacturer's capabilities. For components that are particularly sensitive to mechanical stress, consider using a depanelization method that reduces stress on the board and solder joints. 5. Connecting Adjacent PCB Pads When adjacent pads must be connected to the same net, the copper connections and trace widths should be planned carefully. Poorly designed copper connections may reduce the effective clearance between pads and increase the risk of solder bridging. During PCB layout, maintain adequate electrical clearance between pads and select trace widths according to current-carrying requirements. For fine-pitch components, pay particular attention to the relationship between pads, traces, and solder mask openings to avoid problems with solder paste printing and soldering quality. After completing the layout, run design rule checks (DRC) and verify that the design meets the PCB manufacturer's fabrication and assembly requirements. 6. Thermal Relief vs. Solid Copper Connections When a pad is connected to a copper plane, the connection method should be selected based on soldering requirements, current-carrying capacity, and thermal performance. Two common methods are thermal relief connections and solid copper connections. A thermal relief connection uses several narrow copper spokes to connect the pad to the surrounding copper plane. This reduces heat transfer from the pad into the larger copper area during soldering, making soldering and rework easier in many cases. A solid copper connection directly connects the pad to the copper plane. It generally provides lower electrical and thermal resistance, but the larger copper area can draw heat away from the pad, making it more difficult to reach the required soldering temperature. The appropriate method depends on current requirements, heat dissipation, soldering processes, and rework needs. For high-current or thermally demanding connections, do not reduce the number or width of copper spokes solely to make soldering easier without evaluating the electrical and thermal consequences. 7. Using Teardrops in PCB Layout When a trace connects to a pad or via through a narrow junction, a teardrop can be added where appropriate to create a smoother transition between the trace and the connection point. Teardrops offer several potential benefits: Improved connection reliability: They increase the copper area at the trace-to-pad junction, helping reduce the risk of a weakened or broken connection caused by drill misalignment, manufacturing tolerances, or mechanical stress. Enhanced mechanical robustness: The wider transition can make the connection less vulnerable to local narrowing or separation. Improved appearance: Teardrops create a smoother visual transition between traces and pads. However, teardrops are not necessary in every situation. For high-speed or impedance-sensitive traces, engineers should evaluate whether the resulting geometric changes could affect impedance continuity or signal integrity. 8. Trace Width at Component Pads During PCB layout, trace widths near component pads should be selected according to the electrical and mechanical requirements of the design. For differential signals, symmetrical analog circuits, and connections requiring balanced current distribution, trace symmetry, width matching, and length matching may be important for maintaining signal integrity and circuit performance. However, ordinary signal traces do not always need to have identical widths on both sides of a pad. Trace widths should be determined by current-carrying capacity, impedance requirements, pad dimensions, and manufacturing capabilities. Avoid unnecessary abrupt changes in trace width near pad connections. 9. Handling Unused IC Pins Unused IC pins must be handled according to the device datasheet and application requirements. They should not all be connected to ground or left floating indiscriminately. For example: NC pins: Follow the datasheet instructions. Some pins must remain unconnected and should not be grounded without authorization. Unused input pins: Connect them to the specified logic level or use the recommended pull-up, pull-down, or other biasing method to prevent undefined input states. Unused output pins: Do not connect them directly to ground or a power rail unless the datasheet explicitly permits it. Pins permitted to float: Leave them unconnected only when this is allowed or required by the device documentation. For physical pins that are present on the IC but not used in the application, ensure that the PCB footprint correctly represents the actual package. Whether the corresponding pads should be connected to ground or handled in another way depends on the pin function and the device manufacturer's recommendations. Adding a pad and connecting it to ground does not necessarily provide effective shielding. An incorrect connection may instead cause a short circuit or interfere with normal device operation. 10. Via-in-Pad Design Considerations During PCB layout, placing a conventional open via directly within a pad can cause solder to flow into the hole during assembly. This may result in insufficient solder at the joint, poor soldering quality, or other assembly defects. For ordinary SMT pads, avoid placing untreated open vias directly within the pads, particularly for fine-pitch components, unless the manufacturing process supports the design. However, vias are not universally prohibited within pads. Via-in-pad is a common design approach for packages such as BGAs, where routing density and electrical performance may require it. Depending on the application, via filling, capping, or other appropriate via treatments may be needed to prevent solder loss and ensure reliable assembly. Select the appropriate approach based on the component package, via structure, and PCB manufacturer's process capabilities. 11. PCB Edge Clearance for Traces, Pads, and Components Copper traces, pads, and components should maintain adequate clearance from PCB edges to prevent damage during fabrication, depanelization, and subsequent assembly. If copper features or pads are too close to the board edge, routing, V-scoring, or other depanelization processes may damage the copper, expose conductors, or compromise electrical reliability. For single-sided boards and substrates with relatively low mechanical strength, additional attention should be paid to structural integrity and component placement near the edges. The required PCB edge clearance should be determined according to the board material, thickness, depanelization method, and manufacturer's capabilities. Include these clearances in the PCB design rules and verify them before manufacturing. 12. Keep Electrolytic Capacitors Away from Heat Sources Electrolytic capacitors are sensitive to operating temperature. Prolonged exposure to elevated temperatures can accelerate electrolyte loss and shorten capacitor service life. During PCB layout, avoid placing electrolytic capacitors too close to power resistors, power semiconductors, transformers, or other heat-generating components whenever possible. If close placement is unavoidable, evaluate the thermal impact based on component temperature rise, airflow direction, and the actual operating environment. Also consider the capacitor's rated operating temperature, ripple current, and self-heating to ensure that it operates within acceptable limits under real-world conditions. Distance from a heat source alone is not sufficient to determine whether a capacitor is safe. Thermal design and the operating conditions of the complete product must also be considered. Conclusion PCB layout affects not only electrical performance but also manufacturability, soldering quality, and long-term reliability. In addition to routing and component placement, engineers should consider assembly processes, mechanical stress, thermal requirements, and the recommendations provided in component datasheets. After completing the PCB design, perform design rule checks and verify the layout against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities and assembly requirements. Careful attention to these PCB layout guidelines can help reduce design issues and improve PCB fabrication and assembly reliability Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout Clock Circuit Design Guidelines for PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 06,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout clock circuit crystal oscillator pcb Layout pcb clock signal routing Clock circuits play an essential role in electronic systems by providing timing signals that synchronize the operation of different components. However, improper clock circuit design can lead to signal interference, timing errors, and system instability. This article explores the PCB design guidelines for crystal circuits, active oscillators, and clock distributors, covering key considerations for component placement, signal routing, and noise reduction. 1. Crystal A clock is an essential part of any electronic system. It acts like the heartbeat of the system, providing synchronization signals to different components. If the clock signal becomes unstable or fails, the entire system may malfunction or stop working. Therefore, proper clock circuit design is essential in PCB design. Common clock sources and distribution components used in PCBs include crystals, oscillators, and clock distributors. Some ICs may generate their own clock signals internally. However, the clock signal ultimately originates from a crystal, an oscillator, or another clock source before being distributed to other components. When designing a crystal circuit, consider the following guidelines: Place the crystal as close as possible to the IC's oscillator pins to minimize trace length and reduce external interference. For designs with high electromagnetic compatibility requirements, consider using a crystal with a metal shield package. Ensure that the shield is properly grounded according to the component datasheet. Avoid routing other signal traces beneath the crystal and its load capacitors, especially high-speed digital signals. A continuous GND reference plane can be provided beneath the crystal circuit according to the IC manufacturer's layout recommendations. Keep high-speed digital signal traces away from the crystal to reduce crosstalk. Keep the ground connections of the load capacitors as short as possible to minimize parasitic inductance and provide a low-impedance return path. Verify Now Blog > Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid Differential Pair Routing: 3 Common Design Mistakes to Avoid by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout Differential Pair Differential Pair Routing High-Speed PCB Design Differential Pair Routing In high-speed PCB design , differential pairs are increasingly used, especially in high-speed interfaces such as USB, HDMI, and PCIe. These interfaces commonly use differential signaling for reliable data transmission. Why is differential signaling so widely used? Compared with conventional single-ended routing, differential pairs offer better noise immunity, help suppress common-mode noise and electromagnetic interference (EMI), and improve signal integrity and timing performance. Differential Pair Routing Requirements In PCB design, a differential pair consists of two closely coupled signal traces. To ensure signal transmission quality, these traces generally need to have matched lengths, equal widths, consistent spacing, and symmetrical routing. Differential impedance must also be controlled according to the design requirements. （Differential Pair Routing Requirements） 1. Equal Length Equal length means keeping the two traces in a differential pair as close in length as possible. The purpose is to control the propagation delay difference (skew) between the two signals, maintain proper timing alignment, and reduce signal imbalance and the resulting common-mode noise. 2. Equal Width and Spacing Equal width means maintaining the same trace width for both signals. Equal spacing means keeping the distance between the two traces as consistent as possible, allowing them to run symmetrically and in parallel. This helps maintain a stable coupling relationship between the two traces, minimizes differential impedance variations, and improves signal transmission quality. 3. Controlled Differential Impedance When designing a PCB with differential pairs, one of the first steps is to determine the target differential impedance required by the interface and plan the routing accordingly. It is also important to minimize impedance variations along the routing path. Differential impedance is affected by several factors, including trace width, spacing between the two traces, copper thickness, PCB material, and stackup structure. These factors should all be considered during the design process to maintain consistent differential impedance. 4. Maintain a Continuous Reference Plane Although differential signals offer strong noise immunity, they still require an appropriate reference plane. The reference plane beneath the differential pair should remain continuous whenever possible. Avoid routing differential pairs across split ground planes or slots in the reference plane, as these discontinuities can alter return paths and cause impedance variations. Common Misconceptions About Differential Pair Routing Misconception 1: Differential Signals Do Not Need a Ground Plane as a Return Path, or the Two Traces Can Serve as Each Other's Return Paths. Differential signals offer strong immunity to common-mode noise, but this does not mean they do not need a reference plane. In fact, the return-current path depends on the coupling between the two differential traces and their coupling to the reference plane. Differential-mode return current is primarily associated with the electromagnetic coupling between the two traces, while the reference plane still affects the return path and impedance characteristics, especially for common-mode currents. When the reference plane contains splits or slots, the return-current path may change, causing impedance discontinuities, signal degradation, and increased EMI. Therefore, differential pairs should be routed over a continuous reference plane whenever possible, avoiding split ground regions. In addition, removing the reference plane beneath differential traces to suppress common-mode noise is not recommended. This can make impedance control more difficult and disrupt the return path for common-mode currents, potentially increasing electromagnetic radiation. （Differential Signal Reference Plane） Misconception 2: Maintaining Consistent Spacing Is More Important Than Matching Trace Lengths. In practical PCB routing, it is not always possible to satisfy every differential pair design requirement simultaneously. Component pin placement, via locations, and available routing space may require designers to introduce serpentine routing to match trace lengths. However, this can cause some sections of the differential pair to lose their parallel alignment or consistent spacing. In such cases, design priorities should be determined according to the interface specifications and application requirements. For high-speed differential interfaces with strict intra-pair skew limits, length matching is particularly important. However, trace spacing also affects coupling and differential impedance, so it should not be overlooked. During routing, priority should be given to meeting interface timing and impedance requirements. Symmetry, consistent spacing, and routing continuity should then be maintained as much as possible, rather than focusing on just one routing parameter. （Differential Line Length Matching） Misconception 3: Differential Traces Must Always Be Routed Close Together. Routing differential traces close together strengthens the coupling between them, improving noise immunity and helping reduce electromagnetic radiation through partial magnetic field cancellation. However, closer spacing is not always better. The spacing should be determined by the target differential impedance, PCB stackup, and application requirements. Excessively small spacing may make impedance control and manufacturing more challenging. To reduce crosstalk, maintain sufficient spacing between differential pairs and other signal traces. The 4W rule (spacing of at least four times the trace width) can serve as an initial guideline, but actual spacing should be determined by the design requirements. Ground guard traces connected to the reference plane through stitching vias can also provide additional isolation. For high-frequency applications, coplanar waveguide (CPW) structures are another option for controlling differential impedance. （Differential Line Spacing） Conclusion Differential pair routing is an important part of high-speed PCB design . In addition to trace length, width, and spacing, designers must also consider differential impedance, reference-plane continuity, and interference from surrounding signals. Only by considering all these factors together can designers ensure reliable differential signal transmission and improve overall PCB performance and reliability. Controlled Differential Impedance When designing a PCB with differential pairs, one of the first steps is to determine the target differential impedance required by the interface and plan the routing accordingly. It is also important to minimize impedance variations along the routing path. Differential impedance is affected by several factors, including trace width, spacing between the two traces, copper thickness, PCB material, and stackup structure. These factors should all be considered during the design process to maintain consistent differential impedance. 4. Maintain a Continuous Reference Plane Although differential signals offer strong noise immunity, they still require an appropriate reference plane. The reference plane beneath the differential pair should remain continuous whenever possible. Avoid routing differential pairs across split ground planes or slots in the reference plane, as these discontinuities can alter return paths and cause impedance variations. Common Misconceptions About Differential Pair Routing Misconception 1: Differential Signals Do Not Need a Ground Plane as a Return Path, or the Two Traces Can Serve as Each Other's Return Paths. Differential signals offer strong immunity to common-mode noise, but this does not mean they do not need a reference plane. In fact, the return-current path depends on the coupling between the two differential traces and their coupling to the reference plane. Differential-mode return current is primarily associated with the electromagnetic coupling between the two traces, while the reference plane still affects the return path and impedance characteristics, especially for common-mode currents. When the reference plane contains splits or slots, the return-current path may change, causing impedance discontinuities, signal degradation, and increased EMI. Therefore, differential pairs should be routed over a continuous reference plane whenever possible, avoiding split ground regions. In addition, removing the reference plane beneath differential traces to suppress common-mode noise is not recommended. This can make impedance control more difficult and disrupt the return path for common-mode currents, potentially increasing electromagnetic radiation. （Differential Signal Reference Plane） Misconception 2: Maintaining Consistent Spacing Is More Important Than Matching Trace Lengths. In practical PCB routing, it is not always possible to satisfy every differential pair design requirement simultaneously. Component pin placement, via locations, and available routing space may require designers to introduce serpentine routing to match trace lengths. However, this can cause some sections of the differential pair to lose their parallel alignment or consistent spacing. In such cases, design priorities should be determined according to the interface specifications and application requirements. For high-speed differential interfaces with strict intra-pair skew limits, length matching is particularly important. However, trace spacing also affects coupling and differential impedance, so it should not be overlooked. During routing, priority should be given to meeting interface timing and impedance requirements. Symmetry, consistent spacing, and routing continuity should then be maintained as much as possible, rather than focusing on just one routing parameter. （Differential Line Length Matching） Misconception 3: Differential Traces Must Always Be Routed Close Together. Routing differential traces close together strengthens the coupling between them, improving noise immunity and helping reduce electromagnetic radiation through partial magnetic field cancellation. However, closer spacing is not always better. The spacing should be determined by the target differential impedance, PCB stackup, and application requirements. Excessively small spacing may make impedance control and manufacturing more challenging. To reduce crosstalk, maintain sufficient spacing between differential pairs and other signal traces. The 4W rule (spacing of at least four times the trace width) can serve as an initial guideline, but actual spacing should be determined by the design requirements. Ground guard traces connected to the reference plane through stitching vias can also provide additional isolation. For high-frequency applications, coplanar waveguide (CPW) structures are another option for controlling differential impedance. （Differential Line Spacing） Conclusion Differential pair routing is an important part of high-speed PCB design . In addition to trace length, width, and spacing, designers must also consider differential impedance, reference-plane continuity, and interference from surrounding signals. Only by considering all these factors together can designers ensure reliable differential signal transmission and improve overall PCB performance and reliability. NTC, PTC, and PCB Layout by: Mila Nov 18,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout thermistor circuit NTC thermistor PTC thermistor NTC vs PTC thermistor thermistor pcb Temperature monitoring is essential for protecting electronic components, maintaining system stability, and ensuring reliable operation. Whether preventing a battery from overheating or keeping an industrial motor within its operating temperature range, accurate temperature sensing plays an important role. Among various temperature sensors, thermistors are widely used because of their simple structure, low cost, and fast response. This article explains how thermistors work, explores common measurement circuits, discusses key performance parameters, and compares NTC and PTC thermistors to help guide component selection and PCB design . 1. What Is a Thermistor? Understanding How It Works Working Principle: A thermistor is a resistor whose resistance changes significantly with temperature. The name comes from the combination of "thermal" and "resistor." Its key characteristic is that its resistance varies in response to changes in its own temperature. This property allows a thermistor to convert temperature, a physical quantity, into a change in electrical resistance, which can then be converted into a measurable voltage signal through an external circuit. Figure 1. Different types of thermistors Two Main Types: Based on how their resistance changes with temperature, thermistors are generally divided into two categories: NTC (Negative Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance decreases as temperature increases. NTC thermistors are among the most widely used temperature-sensing components due to their low cost and high sensitivity. Common applications include battery temperature monitoring, power management, and household appliance temperature control. PTC (Positive Temperature Coefficient) Thermistors: Their resistance increases as temperature rises. Depending on their materials and resistance characteristics, PTC thermistors can be further divided into two types: Nonlinear (Switching-Type) PTC Thermistors: Their resistance increases sharply near a specific temperature, known as the Curie temperature. They are commonly used for overcurrent protection, overtemperature protection, and resettable fuses. Linear PTC Thermistors: Typically made from silicon, these devices have a relatively stable positive temperature coefficient. Their resistance increases approximately linearly with temperature, making them suitable for temperature measurement applications. Simply put, an NTC thermistor behaves like a component that offers less resistance as it gets hotter. A linear PTC thermistor works in the opposite way: its resistance increases with temperature, generally in a more uniform and predictable manner. 2. How to Read a Thermistor: Two Common Measurement Circuits A thermistor does not generate an electrical signal on its own. It requires an external excitation source to convert its resistance changes into a measurable voltage signal. The following are two commonly used measurement circuits. Voltage Divider Circuit (Constant-Voltage Excitation) Figure 2. Thermistor in a voltage divider configuration This is one of the simplest and most cost-effective thermistor measurement methods. A thermistor is connected in series with a fixed reference resistor and supplied by a stable voltage source, such as VCC. By measuring the voltage across one of the resistors, the temperature information can be obtained. Working Principle: When the temperature changes, the thermistor's resistance changes accordingly. According to the voltage divider principle, the output voltage, V_TEMP, also changes. By measuring this voltage, the thermistor resistance can be calculated, and the corresponding temperature can then be determined. Advantages: The circuit is simple, requires few components, and has a low implementation cost, making it suitable for many conventional temperature-sensing applications. Considerations: Variations in the supply voltage VCC can affect V_TEMP and introduce measurement errors. To reduce this effect, a ratiometric measurement method can be used. For example, the same voltage source can serve as both the excitation voltage for the divider and the ADC reference voltage. This helps cancel out the effects of supply voltage fluctuations. Constant-Current Excitation Circuit Figure 3. Thermistor measurement using constant-current excitation Another approach is to use a precision constant-current source (I BIAS ) to supply a stable current to the thermistor. Working Principle: According to Ohm's law, V = I × R. Since the current flowing through the thermistor remains constant, the voltage across it, V_TEMP, is proportional to its resistance: V TEMP = I BIAS × R THERMISTOR When the temperature changes and the thermistor resistance varies, the output voltage changes accordingly. Advantages: Within the operating range of the current source, the output voltage is linearly proportional to the thermistor resistance. This makes resistance measurement and signal processing more straightforward, especially in applications requiring relatively high measurement accuracy. Considerations: The accuracy, temperature drift, and output voltage range of the current source all affect measurement results. In addition, excessive excitation current can cause thermistor self-heating. Therefore, the bias current must be selected carefully. The Next Step: Signal Processing The resulting analog voltage signal, V TEMP , is typically sent to an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) input on a microcontroller (MCU) for digital processing. Alternatively, it can be sent to a voltage comparator and compared with a preset threshold voltage to implement a basic overtemperature alarm. Figure 4. Overtemperature threshold detection using a thermistor and comparator 3. Key Parameters for Improving Thermistor Performance and Accuracy When selecting a thermistor, its nominal resistance is not the only parameter to consider. The following characteristics also play an important role in determining temperature measurement accuracy, stability, and overall circuit complexity. Resistance Tolerance Resistance tolerance refers to the allowable deviation between a thermistor's actual resistance and its nominal resistance at a specified temperature, typically 25°C. For example, a tolerance of ±1% means the actual resistance can vary within 1% of the specified nominal value at that temperature. NTC Thermistors: The resistance tolerance of an NTC thermistor depends not only on its nominal resistance at 25°C but also on the tolerance of its B-value and other material characteristics. Therefore, even if an NTC thermistor has a resistance tolerance of ±1% at 25°C, its actual measurement error may increase significantly at other temperatures. Linear PTC Thermistors: Some silicon-based linear PTC thermistors maintain relatively stable resistance-temperature characteristics over a wide operating temperature range, helping achieve consistent measurements. However, their actual tolerance still depends on the specific device and its datasheet specifications. Temperature Sensitivity and Measurement Resolution Sensitivity describes how much a thermistor's resistance changes in response to a change in temperature. It reflects the sensor's ability to respond to temperature variations. Measurement resolution, on the other hand, refers to the smallest temperature change that the entire measurement system can detect. NTC Thermistors: The resistance-temperature relationship of an NTC thermistor is nonlinear, and its sensitivity varies with temperature. It generally has higher relative sensitivity at lower temperatures, while its relative sensitivity tends to decrease as temperature rises. Linear PTC Thermistors: Silicon-based linear PTC thermistors typically exhibit a more uniform resistance change with temperature, helping maintain a consistent measurement response across a relatively wide temperature range. It is important to note that the final measurement resolution depends not only on the thermistor itself but also on the ADC resolution, reference voltage, signal noise, and external circuit design. Linearization: Simplifying Circuit Design Ideally, a sensor's output signal should have a linear relationship with the measured temperature. This simplifies subsequent data processing and temperature conversion. Challenges with NTC Thermistors: The resistance-temperature (R-T) relationship of an NTC thermistor is strongly nonlinear. To improve measurement linearity over the operating temperature range, software compensation is commonly used. Alternatively, additional components, such as a parallel resistor, can be added to the circuit for hardware linearization. Both approaches introduce some additional design or computational complexity. Figure 5. Improving the linearity of an NTC measurement circuit by adding a parallel resistor Advantages of Linear PTC Thermistors: Silicon-based linear PTC thermistors have an inherently more linear R-T characteristic, which can reduce the need for nonlinear compensation and simplify temperature conversion. However, the actual linearity of the output voltage relative to temperature also depends on the excitation circuit design. Figure 6. Linear PTC thermistors do not require a parallel resistor Self-Heating and Long-Term Drift Self-Heating: When current flows through a thermistor, Joule heating occurs, causing the device's own temperature to rise above the surrounding ambient temperature. This can introduce errors into temperature measurements. The degree of self-heating depends on the excitation method and the device's thermal dissipation conditions. For example, under constant-current excitation, thermistor power dissipation is: P = I² × R For an NTC thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature rises, so its power dissipation also decreases under constant-current excitation. Under constant-voltage excitation, however, power dissipation is: P = V² / R In this case, a decrease in NTC resistance may cause power dissipation to increase. Therefore, the excitation current or voltage should be properly controlled to prevent self-heating from affecting measurement accuracy. Long-Term Drift: Long-term drift refers to changes in a thermistor's resistance-temperature characteristics after prolonged operation or exposure to environmental factors such as temperature and humidity. It is closely related to the material, manufacturing process, operating temperature, and application environment. When selecting a thermistor, check the long-term stability and aging test data provided in its datasheet. This is particularly important in applications with demanding reliability requirements, such as automotive electronics and industrial control systems. Calibration All temperature sensors may exhibit component-to-component variations and system-level errors. Therefore, calibration is often necessary in applications requiring high measurement accuracy. NTC Thermistors: Because of their nonlinear R-T characteristics and potentially varying resistance errors across different temperatures, two-point or multipoint calibration may be required in applications with a wide temperature range or strict accuracy requirements. Linear PTC Thermistors: Thanks to their relatively linear characteristics, some devices can achieve good measurement accuracy with single-point calibration. However, multipoint calibration may still be necessary when high accuracy is required across the entire operating temperature range. The appropriate calibration method should be determined based on the required accuracy, operating temperature range, and device datasheet. 4. Software Processing: Converting Voltage into Temperature After the MCU reads the ADC value corresponding to V_TEMP, an algorithm is needed to convert it into an actual temperature value. Two common methods are used. Lookup Table Method A lookup table is created in advance to establish the relationship between resistance or ADC values and temperature. The MCU searches the table using the measured value to obtain the corresponding temperature. Interpolation can also be used to improve conversion accuracy. This method offers fast execution and simple implementation, but it requires additional memory. It is a practical option for MCUs with limited computational resources. Equation-Based Calculation Mathematical models are used to fit the thermistor's R-T curve and convert the measured resistance into temperature. For NTC Thermistors: The Steinhart-Hart equation is commonly used: 1/T = A + B*ln(R) + C*[ln(R)]³ Where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin (K), R is the thermistor resistance, and A, B, and C are coefficients determined by the device's characteristics. For Linear PTC Thermistors: If the device has a sufficiently linear resistance-temperature relationship, a simple linear equation can be used: T = T₀ + (R − R₀) / (α × R₀) Where T₀ is the reference temperature, R₀ is the resistance at that temperature, and α is the temperature coefficient. For applications requiring higher accuracy, polynomial fitting or lookup tables can also be used to compensate for deviations from ideal linearity. 5. PCB Layout Considerations for Thermistor Circuits Selecting the right thermistor and designing an appropriate measurement circuit are only part of the process. PCB layout also has a direct impact on temperature measurement accuracy. In precision temperature-sensing applications, sensor placement, signal routing, and grounding all require careful consideration. Proper Thermistor Placement The thermistor's position should be determined by the actual temperature measurement target. If the thermistor is used to monitor the temperature of a MOSFET, power resistor, or power management IC, it should be placed as close as practical to the target heat-generating component to minimize temperature differences caused by thermal conduction paths. If it is used for ambient temperature sensing, it should be kept away from power components, heatsinks, and other significant heat sources to prevent localized heating from affecting the readings. Avoid unnecessary large copper areas or other thermally conductive structures that may transfer heat from nearby components to the thermistor, unless these structures are intentionally part of the thermal sensing design. Optimize Analog Signal Routing The output of a thermistor measurement circuit is an analog signal, which can be affected by electromagnetic interference and noise from other circuits. Keep the signal path between the thermistor and the MCU ADC input as short as practical. Avoid routing the signal parallel to high-frequency clock lines, switching nodes, or high-current traces over long distances. If necessary, add an appropriate RC filter at the ADC input to suppress high-frequency noise. Consider Grounding and ADC Reference Voltage Grounding and reference voltage stability also affect temperature measurement accuracy. Avoid sharing long ground paths between the thermistor measurement circuit and high-current return paths to reduce errors caused by ground potential variations. Ensure that the ADC reference voltage is stable to prevent power supply noise from affecting conversion results. For voltage divider measurement circuits, consider using a ratiometric measurement approach in which the divider supply and ADC reference voltage are the same. This helps reduce errors caused by supply voltage fluctuations. 6. Summary and Thermistor Selection Guide NTC and linear PTC thermistors each have their own advantages. The appropriate choice depends on the measurement temperature range, accuracy requirements, cost, and circuit design complexity. Key Selection Considerations: If cost is a major concern and the measurement range is relatively narrow with moderate accuracy requirements, a traditional NTC thermistor is still an excellent choice. It offers low cost, mature technology, and a wide range of available components. However, its nonlinear characteristics and potential temperature compensation requirements should be taken into account. If an application requires better temperature linearity, stable performance across the operating temperature range, and simpler signal processing, a silicon-based linear PTC thermistor may be worth considering. Its relatively linear characteristics can simplify temperature conversion, but the actual measurement accuracy, operating range, and calibration requirements must still be evaluated based on the specific device specifications. In practical designs, thermistor measurement performance depends not only on the sensor itself but also on the excitation circuit, ADC configuration, sensor placement, and thermistor PCB layout. By considering component selection, circuit design, and PCB layout together, designers can develop more accurate and reliable temperature monitoring systems. Linear PTC thermistors do not require a parallel resistor Self-Heating and Long-Term Drift Self-Heating: When current flows through a thermistor, Joule heating occurs, causing the device's own temperature to rise above the surrounding ambient temperature. This can introduce errors into temperature measurements. The degree of self-heating depends on the excitation method and the device's thermal dissipation conditions. For example, under constant-current excitation, thermistor power dissipation is: P = I² × R For an NTC thermistor, resistance decreases as temperature rises, so its power dissipation also decreases under constant-current excitation. Under constant-voltage excitation, however, power dissipation is: P = V² / R In this case, a decrease in NTC resistance may cause power dissipation to increase. Therefore, the excitation current or voltage should be properly controlled to prevent self-heating from affecting measurement accuracy. Long-Term Drift: Long-term drift refers to changes in a thermistor's resistance-temperature characteristics after prolonged operation or exposure to environmental factors such as temperature and humidity. It is closely related to the material, manufacturing process, operating temperature, and application environment. When selecting a thermistor, check the long-term stability and aging test data provided in its datasheet. This is particularly important in applications with demanding reliability requirements, such as automotive electronics and industrial control systems. Calibration All temperature sensors may exhibit component-to-component variations and system-level errors. Therefore, calibration is often necessary in applications requiring high measurement accuracy. NTC Thermistors: Because of their nonlinear R-T characteristics and potentially varying resistance errors across different temperatures, two-point or multipoint calibration may be required in applications with a wide temperature range or strict accuracy requirements. Linear PTC Thermistors: Thanks to their relatively linear characteristics, some devices can achieve good measurement accuracy with single-point calibration. However, multipoint calibration may still be necessary when high accuracy is required across the entire operating temperature range. The appropriate calibration method should be determined based on the required accuracy, operating temperature range, and device datasheet. 4. Software Processing: Converting Voltage into Temperature After the MCU reads the ADC value corresponding to V_TEMP, an algorithm is needed to convert it into an actual temperature value. Two common methods are used. Lookup Table Method A lookup table is created in advance to establish the relationship between resistance or ADC values and temperature. The MCU searches the table using the measured value to obtain the corresponding temperature. Interpolation can also be used to improve conversion accuracy. This method offers fast execution and simple implementation, but it requires additional memory. It is a practical option for MCUs with limited computational resources. Equation-Based Calculation Mathematical models are used to fit the thermistor's R-T curve and convert the measured resistance into temperature. For NTC Thermistors: The Steinhart-Hart equation is commonly used: 1/T = A + B*ln(R) + C*[ln(R)]³ Where T is the absolute temperature in Kelvin (K), R is the thermistor resistance, and A, B, and C are coefficients determined by the device's characteristics. For Linear PTC Thermistors: If the device has a sufficiently linear resistance-temperature relationship, a simple linear equation can be used: T = T₀ + (R − R₀) / (α × R₀) Where T₀ is the reference temperature, R₀ is the resistance at that temperature, and α is the temperature coefficient. For applications requiring higher accuracy, polynomial fitting or lookup tables can also be used to compensate for deviations from ideal linearity. 5. PCB Layout Considerations for Thermistor Circuits Selecting the right thermistor and designing an appropriate measurement circuit are only part of the process. PCB layout also has a direct impact on temperature measurement accuracy. In precision temperature-sensing applications, sensor placement, signal routing, and grounding all require careful consideration. Proper Thermistor Placement The thermistor's position should be determined by the actual temperature measurement target. If the thermistor is used to monitor the temperature of a MOSFET, power resistor, or power management IC, it should be placed as close as practical to the target heat-generating component to minimize temperature differences caused by thermal conduction paths. If it is used for ambient temperature sensing, it should be kept away from power components, heatsinks, and other significant heat sources to prevent localized heating from affecting the readings. Avoid unnecessary large copper areas or other thermally conductive structures that may transfer heat from nearby components to the thermistor, unless these structures are intentionally part of the thermal sensing design. Optimize Analog Signal Routing The output of a thermistor measurement circuit is an analog signal, which can be affected by electromagnetic interference and noise from other circuits. Keep the signal path between the thermistor and the MCU ADC input as short as practical. Avoid routing the signal parallel to high-frequency clock lines, switching nodes, or high-current traces over long distances. If necessary, add an appropriate RC filter at the ADC input to suppress high-frequency noise. Consider Grounding and ADC Reference Voltage Grounding and reference voltage stability also affect temperature measurement accuracy. Avoid sharing long ground paths between the thermistor measurement circuit and high-current return paths to reduce errors caused by ground potential variations. Ensure that the ADC reference voltage is stable to prevent power supply noise from affecting conversion results. For voltage divider measurement circuits, consider using a ratiometric measurement approach in which the divider supply and ADC reference voltage are the same. This helps reduce errors caused by supply voltage fluctuations. 6. Summary and Thermistor Selection Guide NTC and linear PTC thermistors each have their own advantages. The appropriate choice depends on the measurement temperature range, accuracy requirements, cost, and circuit design complexity. Key Selection Considerations: If cost is a major concern and the measurement range is relatively narrow with moderate accuracy requirements, a traditional NTC thermistor is still an excellent choice. It offers low cost, mature technology, and a wide range of available components. However, its nonlinear characteristics and potential temperature compensation requirements should be taken into account. If an application requires better temperature linearity, stable performance across the operating temperature range, and simpler signal processing, a silicon-based linear PTC thermistor may be worth considering. Its relatively linear characteristics can simplify temperature conversion, but the actual measurement accuracy, operating range, and calibration requirements must still be evaluated based on the specific device specifications. In practical designs, thermistor measurement performance depends not only on the sensor itself but also on the excitation circuit, ADC configuration, sensor placement, and thermistor PCB layout. By considering component selection, circuit design, and PCB layout together, designers can develop more accurate and reliable temperature monitoring systems. Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing PCB Layout Design Process from Schematic to Manufacturing by: Mila Sep 16,2025 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb layout design schematic design pcb layout services pcb layout design services PCB layout design is the process of transforming an electrical schematic into a complete, manufacturable printed circuit board (PCB). A well-designed PCB layout must do more than simply connect components. It needs to balance electrical performance, signal integrity, power integrity, thermal management, mechanical constraints, manufacturability, and reliability. For complex electronic products, decisions made during PCB layout can have a significant impact on product performance, production yield, cost, and time to market. A professional PCB layout workflow therefore requires systematic planning, engineering review, design verification, and manufacturing preparation. Below is an overview of the PCB layout design process we follow, from the initial schematic review to final manufacturing data.You can also find more information on our PCB Layout page . Step 1 – Design Preparation and Engineering Review The PCB layout process begins with a detailed review of the design requirements and source files. Before starting the layout, our engineers review the schematic and project specifications to make sure the design is ready for PCB implementation. This includes checking: Schematic completeness and connectivity Component information and footprints Board dimensions and mechanical constraints Layer count and stack-up requirements Component placement restrictions High-speed and differential signals Power distribution requirements Impedance-control requirements Thermal considerations Manufacturing capabilities and design rules If the customer only provides a PDF or image-based schematic, we can recreate the schematic in professional EDA software before proceeding with PCB layout. If the original schematic file is available, we can directly import the design data, generate the netlist, and establish the PCB design environment. At this stage, we also identify potential design issues that could affect layout, manufacturing, or product performance. Resolving these issues early helps reduce design iterations later in the process. Step 2 – PCB Stack-Up and Design Rule Setup Before component placement and routing, the PCB layer structure and key design rules need to be established. For multilayer and high-speed PCBs, the stack-up directly affects signal integrity, impedance control, power integrity, EMI performance, and manufacturability. Depending on the application, we may define: Number of PCB layers Core and prepreg materials Copper thickness Dielectric thickness Controlled impedance requirements Power and ground reference planes Minimum trace width and spacing Via structures and drill sizes Manufacturing constraints For high-speed designs, impedance-controlled traces and their reference planes are considered from the beginning rather than being treated as an afterthought. The design rules are then configured in the EDA software to ensure that the layout remains consistent with both the electrical requirements and the PCB manufacturer's manufacturing capabilities. Step 3 – Component Placement Component placement is one of the most important stages of PCB layout because it establishes the physical structure of the entire board. The placement strategy typically starts with components whose locations are constrained by the mechanical design, such as: Connectors Switches and buttons Mounting holes Displays Mechanical interfaces Heat sinks and other thermal components Core components such as MCUs, CPUs, FPGAs, memory devices, power ICs, and communication ICs are then positioned according to signal flow, functional relationships, and electrical requirements. Supporting components are placed close to their corresponding devices to minimize unnecessary routing length and improve electrical performance. During placement, we consider several factors simultaneously: Signal Integrity High-speed interfaces and sensitive signals require appropriate component relationships and short, well-controlled routing paths. Power Integrity Decoupling capacitors should be positioned close to the relevant power pins, while power distribution paths should be kept short and low impedance. Thermal Management Heat-generating components need sufficient copper area, thermal vias, airflow consideration, and appropriate spacing from temperature-sensitive devices. EMI/EMC Performance Sensitive analog circuits, high-speed digital circuits, switching power supplies, and other potential noise sources need to be appropriately positioned to reduce interference. Manufacturability Component spacing, assembly orientation, soldering requirements, and accessibility for inspection and rework are also considered. A well-planned placement makes subsequent routing more efficient while improving the overall reliability and manufacturability of the PCB. Step 4 – PCB Routing Once the component placement is finalized, the next stage is PCB routing. Routing is not simply about finding a path between two pads. The routing strategy must consider electrical performance, signal integrity, power distribution, EMI/EMC, and manufacturing constraints. Depending on the design, routing priorities may include: High-Speed and Critical Signals High-speed interfaces such as USB, DDR, PCIe, Ethernet, HDMI, LVDS, and other differential interfaces may require: Controlled impedance Differential-pair routing Length matching Skew control Appropriate reference planes Minimized discontinuities Careful via transitions Critical signals are routed according to their electrical requirements rather than simply following the shortest available path. Power and Ground Power distribution networks are designed to provide stable and low-impedance power delivery. Ground planes are carefully maintained to provide appropriate return paths and reduce unwanted noise and electromagnetic interference. General Signals After critical nets have been addressed, general signal routing is completed according to the defined design rules for: Trace width Trace spacing Via size Clearance Routing layers Manufacturing limitations For dense boards, routing may require multiple iterations of placement and routing optimization to achieve a balance between electrical performance and manufacturability. Step 5– Layout Optimization and Verification After routing is completed, the PCB layout undergoes a detailed optimization and verification process. This stage may include: Copper Pour and Plane Optimization Copper pours and power/ground planes are optimized to improve current return paths, grounding, shielding, and thermal performance. Silkscreen Optimization Reference designators, polarity markings, pin-1 indicators, and other assembly information are adjusted to improve readability and prevent interference with pads or other components. Design Rule Check (DRC) Automated DRC is performed to identify potential violations such as: Clearance violations Trace width violations Unconnected nets Via and drill violations Component spacing issues Copper-to-board-edge violations Other manufacturer-specific rule violations Engineer Review Beyond automated DRC, the layout is also reviewed from an engineering perspective. Depending on the project, this may include checking: Signal integrity Power integrity Thermal performance EMI/EMC considerations High-speed routing Manufacturing constraints Assembly requirements Mechanical compatibility Automated checks can identify rule violations, but they cannot replace engineering judgment. A professional PCB review therefore combines software-based verification with engineering inspection. Step 6 – Design Review and Customer Approval Before generating final manufacturing data, the completed PCB layout is provided to the customer for review. The customer can verify key aspects of the design, including: Component locations Board dimensions Connector positions Mechanical interfaces Silkscreen information Routing and design intent Any required changes are incorporated before the design is released for manufacturing. This review stage provides an important checkpoint between PCB design and production and helps ensure that the final layout accurately reflects the customer's design requirements. Step 7 – Manufacturing Data Generation Once the PCB layout has been approved, the final manufacturing data is generated. Depending on the project, the manufacturing package may include: Gerber files NC drill files PCB fabrication drawings Bill of Materials (BOM) Pick-and-place files Assembly drawings Stack-up information Other manufacturing documentation Gerber files contain the graphical information required to manufacture the PCB, including copper layers, solder mask, silkscreen, and other fabrication layers. For PCB assembly projects, the BOM and pick-and-place files provide the component and placement information required for SMT assembly. Before release, the output files are checked to ensure that the generated manufacturing data is consistent with the approved PCB design. Step 8 – DFM and PCB Manufacturing The final stage is transferring the verified manufacturing data into production. Before fabrication, the manufacturing data can be evaluated against the PCB manufacturer's capabilities through Design for Manufacturability (DFM) checks. Typical DFM considerations include: Minimum trace width and spacing Minimum drill size Copper-to-edge clearance Annular ring requirements Solder mask clearance Via structures Board thickness Copper thickness Surface finish Manufacturing tolerances Manufacturing requirements are considered from the very beginning of PCBWay's PCB layout process, helping minimize production issues and unnecessary manufacturing delays. What’s more, upon completion of the PCB Layout order, free technical support and a permanent 5% discount on PCBA production will be provided. Why Professional PCB Layout Matters PCB layout has a direct impact on the performance and manufacturability of an electronic product. A professional PCB layout should consider the entire product development process—not just whether all components are electrically connected. Depending on the application, the layout may need to address: Signal Integrity (SI) Power Integrity (PI) EMI/EMC Thermal Management High-Speed Design Design for Manufacturability (DFM) Design for Assembly (DFA) Mechanical Integration Reliability and Serviceability The earlier these factors are considered, the fewer problems are likely to appear during prototype validation and mass production. At PCBWay, our PCB design engineers work with customers throughout the layout process, helping transform circuit concepts and schematics into manufacturable, reliable, and production-ready PCB designs. If you are looking for professional PCB layout or PCB design services, feel free to contact us or submit PCB Layout requirement here. Our engineering team can help evaluate your design and develop a PCB layout optimized for both performance and manufacturing.
