Verify Now Blog > PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Soldering Quality PCB Layout Guidelines for Better Soldering Quality by: Mila Nov 04,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout pcb Layout pcb soldering pcb assembly pcb design guidelines PCB design plays an important role in soldering quality and overall assembly reliability. From component placement and pad design to fiducial marks and copper connections, even small layout details can affect solder paste printing, component placement, and reflow soldering. In this article, we'll explore key PCB layout guidelines to help reduce common soldering defects and improve SMT assembly efficiency. Factors Affecting PCB Soldering Quality Producing a high-quality PCB assembly involves multiple stages, from PCB design to component soldering. It requires coordination among PCB designers, process engineers, and production personnel. Several factors can affect PCB soldering quality, including PCB design files, board quality, component quality, oxidation on component leads, solder paste quality, solder paste printing accuracy, pick-and-place programming and placement accuracy, and the reflow oven temperature profile. Among these factors, PCB layout is one of the important elements that directly influence downstream assembly processes. PCB designers may have limited hands-on soldering and manufacturing experience, while production operators at assembly facilities are generally more focused on manufacturing tasks than on analyzing PCB design decisions. If manufacturing and soldering requirements are not considered during the design stage, unnecessary production difficulties may arise. Therefore, PCB designers should consider assembly processes and manufacturing requirements from the beginning to minimize potential problems during production. PCB Design Considerations for Better Soldering The following guidelines cover practical PCB layout considerations that can help reduce soldering defects and improve SMT assembly and repair efficiency. 1. Tooling Holes For PCBs that require SMT assembly, tooling holes can be added according to the requirements of the production equipment. They help secure and position the board during solder paste printing and subsequent manufacturing processes. Tooling holes are generally placed near the board corners or on the tooling edges. When multiple holes are used, their relative positions and machining accuracy should be carefully controlled to avoid positioning errors during production. The number, diameter, and location of tooling holes should be determined based on the PCB dimensions, panelization method, and equipment requirements. Four tooling holes at the corners are not mandatory for every PCB. 2. Fiducial Marks Fiducial marks should be provided on the PCB when required by the SMT equipment. They allow the pick-and-place machine to recognize the board's position and orientation through its vision system, improving component placement accuracy. Fiducial marks are commonly placed diagonally across the PCB and typically use circular exposed copper patterns. Sufficient clearance should be maintained around each mark to prevent nearby copper, pads, or silkscreen graphics from interfering with visual recognition. For double-sided SMT assembly, fiducial marks may be required on both sides, depending on the equipment and assembly process. For panelized PCBs, additional fiducial marks can also be placed on the tooling edges or panel to help the machine identify the entire panel. 3. Fiducial Mark Design Requirements When designing fiducial marks, consider the following points: a. Fiducial marks generally use solid circular exposed copper patterns. Their shape and dimensions should meet the requirements of the pick-and-place machine. b. A typical fiducial mark diameter is approximately 1.0 mm, although the exact size should follow the equipment manufacturer's specifications. c. Maintain a sufficient clearance around each fiducial mark. Avoid placing copper features, pads, silkscreen, or other patterns within this area. A clearance of approximately 1.0 mm around the mark is commonly used, subject to equipment requirements. d. The fiducial mark should provide sufficient contrast against the surrounding PCB surface to ensure reliable visual recognition. e. Keep the fiducial surface clean and flat. Oxidation, contamination, or excessive reflection may affect recognition accuracy. Exposed copper is commonly used, with the surface finish selected according to the PCB manufacturing process. Note that simple silkscreen outlines should not be used as substitutes for fiducial marks. Pick-and-place machines need to recognize a physical feature with a clearly defined boundary and optical characteristics. 4. Maintain Sufficient Clearance from PCB Edges PCB layouts should account for the conveying and clamping requirements of SMT equipment. For boards transported along conveyor rails, sufficient component-free space should be maintained near the board edges to prevent components from interfering with the rails or fixtures. Depending on the equipment, a clearance of approximately 3–5 mm from the board edge may be used as a reference. Avoid placing SMD components, protruding pads, or other features that may interfere with board handling in this area. For double-sided SMT assembly, also consider the risk of component movement or falling during the second reflow process, as well as potential interference between components and conveyor rails. If the PCB is too small to provide sufficient edge clearance, consider adding tooling edges to provide space for board transportation, positioning, and clamping. 5. Avoid Placing Vias Directly in Solder Pads Without Proper Treatment If an untreated via is placed directly within a conventional SMD pad, molten solder may flow into the via during reflow soldering. This can result in insufficient solder at the joint and, in severe cases, lead to weak or unreliable connections. Therefore, vias should generally be avoided directly within ordinary SMD pads. However, Via-in-Pad structures may be necessary for high-density layouts or specific component packages. In such cases, processes such as resin filling and copper capping can be used to prevent solder loss. 6. Polarity Markings for Diodes and Tantalum Capacitors Polarized components, such as diodes and tantalum capacitors, should have clearly defined polarity markings on the PCB to prevent incorrect placement during assembly or manual soldering. Polarity indicators must match the pin definitions in the component datasheet. Standard industry symbols should be used whenever possible. Even when PCB space is limited, ensure that polarity markings remain visible and are not covered by component bodies or other silkscreen graphics. 7. Silkscreen and Component Identification PCB silkscreen should be clear and concise. Avoid excessive component models, specifications, and other text that may make the board difficult to read, especially in high-density layouts. Component reference designators, such as R1, C1, and U1, should be retained whenever possible. They help production personnel identify component locations and make inspection and repair easier. Do not use component descriptions or part numbers without reference designators. This may increase the difficulty of pick-and-place programming and component identification during production. In addition, silkscreen text should not be too small. Place characters away from vias, pads, and other features that may interfere with readability. 8. IC Pad Length For IC packages with exposed leads, such as SOP, PLCC, and QFP, pad length should be determined based on the component lead dimensions and recommended footprint design. Appropriate pad dimensions help ensure proper solder paste printing, solder wetting, and reliable joint formation. They can also provide sufficient access for manual soldering and rework. However, using a fixed ratio, such as 1.5 times the IC lead length, is not recommended as a universal rule. Different package types have different lead structures and dimensions. Always refer to the recommended land pattern in the component datasheet or relevant IPC footprint design guidelines. 9. IC Pad Width For IC packages such as SOP, PLCC, and QFP, pad width and the spacing between adjacent pads directly affect soldering quality. Follow the recommended footprint dimensions in the component datasheet when determining pad width and spacing. Pads that are too wide or have insufficient spacing between them may increase the risk of solder bridging during assembly. For fine-pitch IC packages in particular, careful attention should be paid to pad dimensions, solder paste printing accuracy, and solder mask design. 10. Avoid Arbitrary Component Rotation During PCB layout, pay attention to component orientation and rotation angles. Keeping components of the same type oriented consistently can simplify pick-and-place programming, inspection, and maintenance. It is worth noting that modern pick-and-place machines generally support arbitrary component rotation angles and are not limited to 90°, 180°, or 270° increments. However, component rotation must be consistent with the footprint definition, coordinate files, and placement program. Otherwise, component leads may become misaligned with PCB pads, affecting placement and soldering quality. Pay particular attention to polarity when positioning diodes, electrolytic capacitors, and other polarized components. 11. Connecting Adjacent IC Pins When adjacent IC pins need to be electrically connected, the PCB layout should be designed carefully to avoid soldering problems and make inspection easier. Avoid simply merging multiple pad areas into one large copper region. Instead, use appropriate routing connections and solder mask openings according to the electrical requirements. Ensure that the soldering areas of individual pins remain clearly defined. Sufficient clearance must be maintained between pads that should not be electrically connected to prevent solder bridging. 12. Exposed Thermal Pads Under IC Packages Some IC packages, such as QFN and DFN, have an exposed thermal pad on the underside of the component. This pad is mainly used for heat dissipation and electrical grounding. When designing these packages, follow the recommended thermal pad dimensions in the component datasheet and consider the solder paste stencil design. If the thermal pad is too large and the entire area is covered with solder paste, excessive solder paste may cause problems such as solder voiding, component floating, or solder overflow during reflow. To reduce these risks, the solder paste opening can be divided into multiple smaller sections to control the amount of solder paste deposited. However, the thermal pad should not be arbitrarily reduced simply to prevent short circuits. Thermal performance, electrical connections, and soldering requirements must all be considered. 13. Avoid Placing Two Tall Components Too Close Together Component height and spacing should be considered during PCB layout. If two tall components are placed too close together, the pick-and-place machine may encounter interference when positioning the second component. The first component may obstruct the placement head or nozzle, affecting the placement process. Overcrowded layouts can also make inspection, soldering, and rework more difficult. Therefore, consider component height, package dimensions, nozzle clearance, and maintenance requirements when arranging taller components. Provide sufficient spacing to avoid mechanical interference. 14. BGA Design Considerations BGA components have solder balls underneath the package. Since these solder joints cannot be directly inspected from the outside after assembly, BGA packages require careful attention to PCB pad design, solder paste printing, and reflow soldering. When designing BGA footprints, strictly follow the component datasheet recommendations for pad dimensions, ball pitch, and PCB layout requirements. It is also important to consider inspection and rework requirements in advance. For example, additional positioning features may be needed on the PCB to accommodate BGA rework equipment and fixtures. If auxiliary tooling holes are required, their diameter, location, and spacing should match the actual rework equipment or alignment fixture. A single hole size should not be applied to every BGA design. 15. PCB Solder Mask Color Although solder mask color does not directly determine soldering quality, it may affect the visual recognition performance of SMT equipment. Different solder mask colors have different optical and reflective characteristics, which may influence how the machine's vision system recognizes fiducial marks and component positions. For example, certain dark solder mask colors may provide insufficient contrast under specific lighting conditions. Therefore, when selecting a PCB color, consider not only appearance but also compatibility with the production equipment's vision system. For unusual solder mask colors, confirm compatibility with the PCB manufacturer and SMT assembly provider in advance. 16. Small Components Under Large Components During PCB layout, avoid placing small components underneath large components when doing so may obstruct soldering, inspection, or rework. For example, if resistors or capacitors are placed underneath a seven-segment display or a large connector, technicians may need to remove the larger component before repairing the smaller one if a soldering defect occurs. This increases repair complexity and may damage the larger component or nearby pads during removal. Therefore, when circuit functionality and routing requirements allow, consider placing some small components on the opposite side of the PCB or repositioning them to provide better access for inspection and repair. 17. How Copper Pour Connections Affect Soldering When a PCB pad is directly connected to a large copper pour, heat may dissipate more rapidly during soldering. This can slow down pad heating and affect solder melting and wetting. This is particularly relevant for pads connected to large copper planes or internal power and ground layers. For example, in Figure A, the component pad is directly connected to a large copper area. In Figure B, although the connector pad is not directly connected to the copper pour, the large copper planes in the inner layers may still increase the overall thermal mass and affect soldering. If the reflow temperature is increased to compensate for excessive heat dissipation, temperature-sensitive connectors or plastic components may become deformed. Therefore, for pads that do not require direct high-current connections or special thermal performance, consider using thermal relief connections. These connections use narrow copper spokes to reduce heat dissipation and improve solderability. For high-current pads and thermal pads, however, current-carrying capacity, heat dissipation, and soldering requirements must be considered together. Thermal relief should not be applied indiscriminately. 18. PCB Panelization and Tooling Edge Design For small or irregularly shaped PCBs, panelization can improve SMT production efficiency by allowing multiple boards to be processed together. Several factors should be considered when designing PCB panels: Tooling Edge: Add tooling edges according to the conveying and clamping requirements of SMT equipment. This provides sufficient space for automated assembly. Fiducial Marks: Place fiducial marks on individual boards and the panel when required by the equipment to ensure accurate positioning. Tooling Holes: Add tooling holes as needed to keep the panel stable during manufacturing and assembly. Breakaway Methods: Select an appropriate separation method, such as V-scoring or mouse bites, based on the PCB structure and depanelization requirements. Component Clearance: Maintain sufficient clearance between components and separation areas to prevent mechanical stress from damaging components or solder joints during depanelization. A well-designed PCB panel can improve SMT production efficiency while reducing positioning errors and mechanical damage during assembly. Conclusion PCB layout should consider not only circuit functionality and electrical performance but also downstream manufacturing, soldering, inspection, and repair requirements. Proper fiducial mark placement, pad design, component arrangement, and panelization can help reduce potential problems during solder paste printing, SMT placement, and reflow soldering. PCB designers should therefore take actual manufacturing processes into account from the early design stage. A well-designed PCB should not only meet electrical requirements but also be easy to manufacture and assemble. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Proper fiducial mark placement, pad design, component arrangement, and panelization can help reduce potential problems during solder paste printing, SMT placement, and reflow soldering. Verify Now Blog > Reverse Polarity Protection: Diode, PMOS, NMOS, and Ideal Diode Circuits Reverse Polarity Protection: Diode, PMOS, NMOS, and Ideal Diode Circuits by: Mila Nov 13,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout reverse polarity protection reverse polarity protection circuit MOSFET reverse polarity protection PMOS reverse polarity protection NMOS reverse polarity protection Reverse polarity protection is an important consideration in PCB design , helping prevent damage to electronic components caused by accidentally connecting a power supply with reversed positive and negative terminals. Different reverse polarity protection circuits, including diode-based, PMOS, NMOS, and ideal diode configurations, offer different trade-offs in voltage drop, power dissipation, cost, and circuit complexity. Understanding how these circuits work and how to incorporate them into PCB layouts can help improve power reliability and prevent potential circuit failures. 1. Diode-Based Reverse Polarity Protection Series Schottky Diode A Schottky diode can be connected in series with the power input to provide reverse polarity protection through its unidirectional current-conduction characteristics. Correct polarity: The diode is forward-biased, allowing current to flow through the diode to the load. Reversed polarity: The diode becomes reverse-biased and blocks current from flowing into the downstream circuit, protecting the load. Schottky diodes generally have a lower forward voltage drop than conventional silicon diodes. However, they still introduce voltage and power losses. Therefore, the diode should be selected based on the load current and the allowable input voltage drop. Parallel Diode with a Resettable Fuse This reverse polarity protection circuit uses a diode connected in parallel with the power input and a resettable fuse (PPTC) connected in series with the power supply. Correct polarity: The diode is reverse-biased and normally does not conduct. Current flows through the resettable fuse to the load. Reversed polarity: The diode becomes forward-biased, creating a low-resistance path for the fault current. The resulting current causes the resettable fuse to heat up and enter a high-resistance state, limiting the current and protecting the downstream circuit. Note that this protection method relies on the power supply being capable of delivering sufficient fault current. The diode's forward current rating, the fuse's hold current and trip characteristics, and the power supply's current-limiting capability must all be considered. 2. PMOS Reverse Polarity Protection Series PMOS A PMOS transistor can be used for low-loss reverse polarity protection by taking advantage of its body diode and gate-to-source voltage characteristics. Correct polarity: Current initially flows through the PMOS body diode, creating a voltage difference across the MOSFET. As the source voltage rises, a negative gate-to-source voltage (VGS) develops, turning on the PMOS. Once the MOSFET is fully on, most of the current flows through its channel rather than the body diode, reducing the voltage drop. Reversed polarity: The PMOS turns off, and its body diode becomes reverse-biased, preventing reverse current from flowing into the downstream circuit. Note: Whether the PMOS turns on fully depends on the actual VGS. The threshold voltage alone cannot determine whether the MOSFET is sufficiently enhanced. Ensure that the actual gate-to-source voltage meets the conditions specified for RDS(on) in the datasheet, while remaining within the maximum allowable VGS rating. Under low input voltage conditions, also verify that the voltage remaining after the body diode drop is sufficient to drive the PMOS. Series PMOS with a Zener Diode When the input voltage is relatively high, the PMOS gate-to-source voltage may exceed the maximum rating specified in its datasheet, potentially damaging the gate oxide. To prevent this, a Zener diode and a resistor can be added between the PMOS gate and source to limit VGS. Note: VGS must be sufficient to drive the PMOS while remaining within the maximum rating specified in the datasheet. The Zener voltage should be selected based on the MOSFET's gate-drive requirements and maximum allowable VGS, with an appropriate safety margin. The resistor is generally used to limit the current through the Zener diode and gate circuit. Its value should be calculated based on the circuit parameters. In the schematic, D10 limits the PMOS gate-to-source voltage to prevent VGS from exceeding its safe operating range. PMOS Bridge Circuit (Reverse Polarity Protection + Controlled Switching) This configuration uses two MOSFETs and a transistor-based control circuit to provide both reverse polarity protection and power switching. The EN logic should be verified against the actual schematic rather than inferred from the component names. In particular, check the source and drain connections of both MOSFETs, as well as the orientation of their body diodes. In a back-to-back MOSFET configuration, the two body diodes are generally connected in opposite directions so that current can be blocked in both directions when the MOSFETs are off. Operating conditions to verify: Correct polarity, EN active: The MOSFETs turn on or off according to the control circuit. Correct polarity, EN inactive: The MOSFETs turn off, disconnecting the power supply from the load. Reversed polarity: The control circuit should keep the MOSFETs off to prevent reverse current from flowing into the downstream circuit. The original schematic can be retained, but the EN=0 and EN=1 logic should be checked before specifying the exact switching states. 3. NMOS Reverse Polarity Protection NMOS transistors can also be used for reverse polarity protection. Compared with PMOS devices, NMOS transistors generally offer lower on-resistance, making them advantageous in high-current applications. The basic operating principle also relies on the MOSFET body diode and gate-to-source voltage control. Correct polarity: The body diode initially conducts, establishing the conditions for gate drive. The gate-to-source voltage (VGS) then reaches a sufficient level to turn on the MOSFET. Once the channel conducts, the voltage drop across the circuit is reduced. Reversed polarity: The MOSFET turns off, and its body diode becomes reverse-biased, blocking reverse current. Note that NMOS gate driving differs from PMOS gate driving. For a high-side NMOS configuration, the gate voltage must be sufficiently higher than the source voltage to fully turn on the MOSFET. An additional charge pump or boost driver is usually required. For a low-side NMOS configuration, the interruption of the load's ground connection must be taken into account. 4. Soft-Start Circuit A soft-start circuit limits inrush current when the power supply is first connected, preventing input capacitors from charging too rapidly and placing excessive stress on the power supply and switching components. In the illustrated circuit, the capacitor charging process controls the change in the MOSFET gate-to-source voltage. At power-up: The capacitor begins charging from its initial state. The initial circuit conditions determine the MOSFET's gate-to-source voltage, and the circuit is generally designed to keep the MOSFET off or only slightly on. During capacitor charging: The gate voltage gradually changes, and VGS approaches the level required to turn on the MOSFET. The MOSFET gradually enters conduction. At steady state: The MOSFET becomes fully enhanced, and the circuit enters normal operation. The capacitance of C1 affects the RC time constant, which in turn influences the gate voltage transition and startup process. However, the actual soft-start time also depends on the gate resistance, MOSFET gate charge, load capacitance, and circuit topology. In addition, the MOSFET may operate in its linear region during the soft-start period. Its instantaneous power dissipation and safe operating area (SOA) must therefore be considered. 5. Ideal Diode Circuit for Reverse Polarity Protection The Raspberry Pi Model B+ uses a MOSFET-based protection circuit that functions similarly to an ideal diode. Its main characteristics are: VA ≈ VB, with a very small voltage drop during normal operation. Current flows only from A to B. When the output voltage exceeds the input voltage, the circuit can turn off the MOSFET to prevent reverse current. Working Principle This circuit uses matched PNP transistors to form a voltage-sensing and control circuit. By detecting the voltage difference between the input and output terminals, the circuit controls the MOSFET gate voltage to achieve ideal-diode-like unidirectional conduction. The operating process is as follows: 1. When Vin > Vout The input voltage is higher than the output voltage. The PNP control circuit provides the appropriate gate-to-source drive voltage to turn on the MOSFET, allowing current to flow from Vin to Vout. At this point, most of the current flows through the MOSFET channel. The voltage drop is primarily determined by the MOSFET's on-resistance, resulting in lower power loss than a conventional diode. 2. When Vin < Vout When the output voltage becomes higher than the input voltage, the PNP control circuit changes the MOSFET gate state and turns it off, preventing current from flowing backward from Vout to Vin. Therefore, this circuit can provide not only reverse polarity protection but also protection against reverse current between different power sources. For example, when a Raspberry Pi is powered simultaneously through its USB port and GPIO expansion interface, a voltage difference between the two power sources may cause reverse current to flow. An ideal diode circuit can help reduce this risk. Conclusion Choosing the right reverse polarity protection circuit depends on the input voltage, load current, allowable voltage drop, and overall protection requirements. Whether using a diode, PMOS, NMOS, or ideal diode configuration, proper component selection and PCB layout are essential for reliable operation. During PCB layout , pay attention to current paths, trace width, component placement, and thermal management to minimize power losses and ensure effective protection. A well-designed reverse polarity protection circuit helps improve the safety and reliability of the entire PCB. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. USB Type-C Pinout: Why Are 5.1KΩ Pull-Down Resistors Needed? by: Mila Nov 09,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout USB Type-C pinout 5.1K pull-down resistor USB-C CC pin USB Type-C has become a common interface in modern electronic devices thanks to its reversible design, high-speed data transfer, and high-power delivery capabilities. However, in USB Type-C circuit design , a seemingly simple 5.1KΩ pull-down resistor plays an important role in device identification, connection detection, and power delivery. This article explains how the CC pins work, why two 5.1KΩ resistors are needed, and what to consider when designing a USB Type-C interface. Basic Functions of USB Type-C Pins: Understanding the CC Pins The CC (Configuration Channel) pins are among the most important pins in a USB Type-C connector. They are responsible for several key functions: Device Role Identification: Identify the power source (Source/DFP) and power sink (Sink/UFP). Plug Orientation Detection: Detect the orientation of the USB Type-C plug. Power Capability Identification: Determine the available default power level through the Rp resistor when USB PD is not used. USB PD Communication: Enable bidirectional communication through the CC pins for USB Power Delivery. By monitoring the voltage on the CC pin, the Source can determine whether a compatible Sink device has been connected. 2. Sharing One Pull-Down Resistor: Connecting CC1 and CC2 to a single resistor may cause plug orientation detection problems and compatibility issues with some E-Marker cables. 3. Using the Wrong Resistance: Non-standard values such as 10KΩ or 20KΩ may cause the CC voltage to fall outside the specified detection range, affecting device identification and power delivery. Configuring separate Rd resistors for CC1 and CC2 allows Sink devices to establish connections according to the USB Type-C specification and communicate correctly with the Source. For PCB engineers, USB Type-C PCB design involves more than connecting data and power lines. Understanding how the CC pins work and properly configuring Rp and Rd resistors are equally important to avoiding device detection and power delivery issues. As USB Type-C and USB PD technologies continue to gain wider adoption, the CC pins remain essential for device connection, power negotiation, and cable identification. Getting these details right is fundamental to improving the reliability and compatibility of USB Type-C interfaces. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. Verify Now Blog > What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit by: Mila Nov 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout crystal oscillator circuit crystal oscillator circuit design crystal oscillator pcb layout crystal oscillator design In crystal oscillator circuit design , you may notice that some circuits include a 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while others do not. Why is this resistor used, and what happens if it is omitted? Although both configurations can work normally, the feedback resistor can play an important role in establishing the proper operating conditions for reliable crystal startup. Two Common Crystal Oscillator Circuit Configurations In actual product development, you may encounter two different configurations when designing a crystal oscillator circuit. In Figure 1, there is no 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while Figure 2 shows a 1MΩ resistor connected across the crystal. Figure 1: Crystal oscillator circuit with a parallel 1MΩ resistor Figure 2: Crystal oscillator circuit without a parallel 1MΩ resistor Problem Description In some circuit designs, the system operates normally when a 1MΩ resistor is connected in parallel with the crystal. However, without this resistor, the program may start slowly, run abnormally, or even fail to start. Why Is a 1MΩ Resistor Used in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit? 1. How Does the 1MΩ Feedback Resistor Work? In a typical Pierce crystal oscillator circuit, the MCU's internal inverter acts as an amplifier. For the circuit to oscillate reliably, the inverter must operate within its linear region, where it can provide sufficient gain. The 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal serves as a feedback resistor. It provides a DC feedback path and helps establish a suitable bias point for the inverter without significantly loading the oscillation signal. 2. Why Can Some Crystal Oscillators Work Without a 1MΩ Resistor? Not every crystal oscillator circuit requires an external 1MΩ feedback resistor. Some MCUs already integrate the necessary feedback or bias circuitry. In these designs, the internal circuit can establish the appropriate operating point without an additional external resistor. However, if the feedback path is insufficient, the inverter may not operate at the intended bias point. This can result in: Slow crystal startup. Unstable oscillation. Failure to start. 3. How Does Temperature Affect Crystal Oscillator Startup? Temperature changes can affect both the crystal and the MCU's internal oscillator characteristics. For example, the crystal's equivalent series resistance (ESR) and the inverter's electrical characteristics may vary with temperature. These changes can reduce the oscillator's startup margin. If the oscillator loop cannot provide sufficient gain and negative resistance to overcome the crystal's ESR, startup may become slower or fail altogether. When troubleshooting such problems, check the MCU datasheet and reference circuit first. The crystal's ESR, load capacitance, and oscillator drive capability should also be evaluated. 4. Should a Series Resistor Be Added to the Crystal Circuit? Some crystal oscillator designs include a small series resistor, such as 100Ω, to limit the crystal's drive level or adjust the oscillator loop gain. However, this resistor is not required in every design. Its value depends on the crystal's drive-level specification, ESR, and the MCU's oscillator characteristics. An excessively large series resistance may reduce loop gain, making the crystal harder to start. Note: The feedback resistor and series resistor should not be selected arbitrarily. Always follow the MCU and crystal manufacturers' recommendations and verify startup reliability through testing under different operating temperature conditions. PCB Layout Considerations for Crystal Oscillator Circuits In addition to component selection, proper crystal oscillator PCB layout is essential for reliable operation. Consider the following points during crystal oscillator circuit design: Place the crystal as close as possible to the MCU's oscillator pins. Keep the traces between the crystal and load capacitors as short as possible. Minimize the loop area of the oscillator circuit. Keep high-speed signal traces, switching power supply nodes, and other potential noise sources away from the crystal circuit. Follow the chip manufacturer's reference layout when designing the ground plane beneath the crystal. Avoid applying a universal copper-pour rule without considering the specific oscillator design. Verify Now Blog > What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit by: Mila Nov 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout PCB layout crystal oscillator circuit crystal oscillator circuit design crystal oscillator pcb layout crystal oscillator design In crystal oscillator circuit design , you may notice that some circuits include a 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while others do not. Why is this resistor used, and what happens if it is omitted? Although both configurations can work normally, the feedback resistor can play an important role in establishing the proper operating conditions for reliable crystal startup. Two Common Crystal Oscillator Circuit Configurations In actual product development, you may encounter two different configurations when designing a crystal oscillator circuit. In Figure 1, there is no 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal, while Figure 2 shows a 1MΩ resistor connected across the crystal. Figure 1: Crystal oscillator circuit with a parallel 1MΩ resistor Figure 2: Crystal oscillator circuit without a parallel 1MΩ resistor Problem Description In some circuit designs, the system operates normally when a 1MΩ resistor is connected in parallel with the crystal. However, without this resistor, the program may start slowly, run abnormally, or even fail to start. Why Is a 1MΩ Resistor Used in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit? 1. How Does the 1MΩ Feedback Resistor Work? In a typical Pierce crystal oscillator circuit, the MCU's internal inverter acts as an amplifier. For the circuit to oscillate reliably, the inverter must operate within its linear region, where it can provide sufficient gain. The 1MΩ resistor connected in parallel with the crystal serves as a feedback resistor. It provides a DC feedback path and helps establish a suitable bias point for the inverter without significantly loading the oscillation signal. 2. Why Can Some Crystal Oscillators Work Without a 1MΩ Resistor? Not every crystal oscillator circuit requires an external 1MΩ feedback resistor. Some MCUs already integrate the necessary feedback or bias circuitry. In these designs, the internal circuit can establish the appropriate operating point without an additional external resistor. However, if the feedback path is insufficient, the inverter may not operate at the intended bias point. This can result in: Slow crystal startup. Unstable oscillation. Failure to start. 3. How Does Temperature Affect Crystal Oscillator Startup? Temperature changes can affect both the crystal and the MCU's internal oscillator characteristics. For example, the crystal's equivalent series resistance (ESR) and the inverter's electrical characteristics may vary with temperature. These changes can reduce the oscillator's startup margin. If the oscillator loop cannot provide sufficient gain and negative resistance to overcome the crystal's ESR, startup may become slower or fail altogether. When troubleshooting such problems, check the MCU datasheet and reference circuit first. The crystal's ESR, load capacitance, and oscillator drive capability should also be evaluated. 4. Should a Series Resistor Be Added to the Crystal Circuit? Some crystal oscillator designs include a small series resistor, such as 100Ω, to limit the crystal's drive level or adjust the oscillator loop gain. However, this resistor is not required in every design. Its value depends on the crystal's drive-level specification, ESR, and the MCU's oscillator characteristics. An excessively large series resistance may reduce loop gain, making the crystal harder to start. Note: The feedback resistor and series resistor should not be selected arbitrarily. Always follow the MCU and crystal manufacturers' recommendations and verify startup reliability through testing under different operating temperature conditions. PCB Layout Considerations for Crystal Oscillator Circuits In addition to component selection, proper crystal oscillator PCB layout is essential for reliable operation. Consider the following points during crystal oscillator circuit design: Place the crystal as close as possible to the MCU's oscillator pins. Keep the traces between the crystal and load capacitors as short as possible. Minimize the loop area of the oscillator circuit. Keep high-speed signal traces, switching power supply nodes, and other potential noise sources away from the crystal circuit. Follow the chip manufacturer's reference layout when designing the ground plane beneath the crystal. Avoid applying a universal copper-pour rule without considering the specific oscillator design. Why Are Two MOSFETs Connected Back-to-Back in a MOSFET Circuit? by: Mila Nov 12,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout mosfet circuit MOSFET Body Diode Back-to-Back MOSFETs Bidirectional MOSFET Switch Reverse Current Blocking In PCB design , MOSFETs are widely used in power management circuits to control current flow, protect power sources, and manage power switching. However, when a circuit needs to support both charging and discharging while preventing unwanted reverse current, a single MOSFET may not be sufficient. This is where two back-to-back MOSFETs come into play. By connecting two MOSFETs in series with oppositely oriented body diodes, designers can create a bidirectional switch that allows current to flow in both directions when turned on and blocks current in either direction when turned off. This article explains how this configuration works and why it is useful in PCB power circuit design. 1. What Is a Bidirectional Switch? A bidirectional switch is a switching circuit built using MOSFETs, IGBTs, or other power semiconductor devices. It allows current to flow in either direction when turned on and blocks current in both directions when turned off. For example, when point A has a positive voltage and point B has a negative voltage, current can flow from A to B. When the voltage polarity reverses, with A becoming negative and B positive, the current direction also reverses, allowing current to flow from B to A. A bidirectional switch can be constructed by connecting two MOSFETs or IGBTs back-to-back. （Back-to-back MOSFET circuit） So, how does this configuration allow current to flow in both directions? 2. How Do Back-to-Back MOSFETs Enable Bidirectional Conduction? Let's use a circuit that supports both USB-to-battery charging and battery-to-USB power delivery as an example. Charging the Battery from USB When the USB power source charges the battery, the USB-side voltage is higher than the battery-side voltage. In this condition, Q3 turns on, and the USB power source establishes an initial current path through the body diode of Q1 and Q3. The control circuit then applies sufficient gate drive voltage to Q1 and Q2, turning both MOSFETs on. Once both MOSFETs are on, current flows through their conducting channels to the battery, allowing it to charge. Powering a USB Load from the Battery When the battery supplies power to an external USB load, the current flows in the opposite direction. Q3 turns on, allowing an initial current path to form through the body diode of Q2 and Q3. The control circuit then drives Q1 and Q2 on, allowing current to flow through both MOSFET channels toward the USB interface and power the external load. Blocking Reverse Current When Turned Off When Q3 is turned off, the charging and discharging paths are interrupted. The USB power source can no longer charge the battery, and the battery can no longer supply power to the external USB load. This provides reverse current blocking, also known as reverse current protection, preventing unwanted current from flowing back into the power source. It is important to note that the body diode does not automatically turn on the MOSFET channel. Actual MOSFET conduction depends on the gate-to-source voltage (VGS) and the control circuit's operating logic. （The Principle of Reverse Current Blocking） 3. Why Use Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs Instead of One? To understand this, we first need to look at an important MOSFET characteristic: the body diode. A MOSFET has an intrinsic body diode. In a typical N-channel enhancement-mode MOSFET, the body diode's anode is connected to the source (S), and its cathode is connected to the drain (D). This means that even when the MOSFET is turned off, its body diode can still conduct current under the right voltage conditions. Using a Single MOSFET When only one MOSFET is used, turning it off closes its conducting channel, but the body diode remains present. For example, suppose the battery is connected to the source side of the MOSFET and the external load is connected to the drain side. If the source voltage becomes higher than the drain voltage by enough to forward-bias the body diode, the diode conducts. Current can still flow from the battery to the external load through the body diode, so the MOSFET cannot fully block current in this direction. Therefore, a single MOSFET can conduct current in both directions when turned on, but it cannot block current in both directions when turned off. Using Two Back-to-Back MOSFETs When two MOSFETs are connected back-to-back, their body diodes face opposite directions. When both MOSFETs are turned on, their conducting channels are enabled, allowing current to flow from either side to the other. This provides bidirectional conduction. When both MOSFETs are turned off, the oppositely oriented body diodes provide bidirectional blocking. Regardless of which side has the higher voltage, one of the body diodes will be reverse-biased, preventing current from flowing through the series path. Therefore, two back-to-back MOSFETs can provide both bidirectional conduction and bidirectional blocking. Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs The main differences between these two configurations can be summarized as follows: （Single MOSFET vs. Back-to-Back MOSFETs） Conclusion Back-to-back MOSFETs provide an effective way to achieve bidirectional switching and reverse current blocking in power management circuits. Unlike a single MOSFET, this configuration can block current in either direction when turned off while allowing bidirectional conduction when both MOSFETs are on. For PCB design , understanding MOSFET body diode orientation and the operating states of each MOSFET is essential when designing battery charging and discharging circuits, power-path management systems, and other applications that require reliable current control. Proper component selection and gate-drive control are also important to ensure the circuit operates as intended. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. NTC, PTC, and PCB Layout What Is the Purpose of a 1MΩ Resistor in a Crystal Oscillator Circuit Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. Zinc Plating Provides uniform zinc coating which offers protection from corrosion, oxidation, and wear on irregular surfaces. Conforms to ASTM B633-15. What is CNC Machining? CNC, or computer numerical control machining, is a widely used manufacturing process that uses automated, high-speed cutting tools to form designs from metal or plastic stock. Standard CNC machines include 3-axis, 4-axis, and 5-axis milling machines, lathes, and routers. Machines may vary in how CNC machined parts are cut—the workpiece may remain in place while the tool moves, the tool may remain in place while the workpiece is rotated and moved, or both the cutting tool and workpiece may move together. Skilled machinists operate a CNC machine by programming tool paths based on the geometry of the final machined parts. The part geometry information is provided by a CAD (computer-aided design) model. CNC machines can cut almost any metal alloy and rigid plastic with high precision and repeatability, making custom CNC machined parts suitable for nearly every industry, including aerospace , medical, robotics, electronics, and industrial. Xometry provides CNC services and offers custom CNC quotes on over 40 materials ranging from commodity aluminum and acetal to advanced titanium and engineered plastics like PEEK and Teflon. Get More Tips With Our Complete Design Guide Download CNC Guide CNC Machining FAQs How does CNC machining work? CNC machining uses subtractive processes , which means feedstock is machined to its final form by subtracting and removing material. Holes are drilled, lots and pathways are bored, and metal stock is shaped into new material with varying tapers, diameters, and shapes. For subtractive manufacturing, shapes are achieved by the subtraction of material. This contrasts with other types such as additive manufacturing — where materials are added, layered, and deformed to a specified shape. It also contrasts with injection molding where the material is injected in a different state of matter, using a mold, and formed to a specified shape. CNC machining is versatile — and can be used with various materials , including metals, plastics, wood, glass, foam, and other composite materials. This versatility has helped make CNC machining a popular choice across industries , enabling designers and engineers to fabricate products efficiently and precisely. How does CNC machining differ from traditional machining? In traditional machining, a skilled machinist operates a machine, removing or forming metal. This is done according to specifications provided by designers and engineers, usually through an engineering drawing or blueprint. They use turn wheels, dials, switches, chucks, vices, and a variety of cutting tools made of hardened steel, carbide, and industrial diamond, then use measurement instruments to ensure all of the dimensions are correct. CNC machining performs the same function as traditional machining — metal cutting, drilling, milling, boring, grinding, and other metal forming and removal functions — but CNC machines use computer numerical control rather than manual control by a machinist. It is automated, driven by code, and developed by programmers. It is about as precise the first time of cutting as the 500th. Widely used in digital manufacturing (and sometimes in low-volume production runs), it can be revised and altered for modifications and different materials . This type of machining is much more precise and has superseded traditional machining (though not entirely) in manufacturing, fabrication, and industrial production. It uses mathematical coordinates and computing power to achieve the same end with the greatest accuracy. Specifically, computer numerical control uses Cartesian coordinates. These are spatial coordinates — in several dimensions — using coordinates and axes. The automation of cutting tool machines controls its cutting, boring, drilling, or other operation using the numerical control of a computer that reads the coordinates. These coordinates were designated by engineers in the product’s digital drawing and design. What industries use CNC machining? CNC machining is widely used across industries. It is common in aerospace, automotive, consumer electronics, robotics, agriculture, and other fields that frequently use metal parts. It is also widely used in medical devices , household goods, energy, oil and gas, and other consumer applications. It is one of the most common manufacturing processes in the world. What is the history of CNC machining? During World War II, the United States was quickly churning out ships, aircraft, and vehicles for the military. And even once the war ended, production kept up as the country experienced a post-war boom in home construction, infrastructure expansion, and transportation. Naturally, engineers and designers needed tools to help them efficiently meet the growing demand for industrial products. Enter CNC machining . John T. Parsons, who worked in the production of helicopter rotor blades, was one of the first people to champion CNC machining. He and his colleagues at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio used interpolation curves, which could be applied to machining with computational methods, to achieve the complex tapers required for rotor blades. As Parsons’ company got called upon to make more and more complex aircraft parts, they turned to computational methods and cnc machined parts to achieve their desired shapes. This was partly the genesis of CNC machining. Building off of Parsons’ innovations, MIT’s Servomechanisms Laboratory later developed a working machine able to use computational methods to fabricate precise machine parts. Their servo-mechanisms were able to use the Cartesian coordinates — the numerical control — to steer the machine and its moving parts, to fabricate with automated precision. Such automation only grew more sophisticated through the rest of the twentieth century and continues to develop today. What are your inspection options for CNC machining? All machined and sheet metal parts will receive a standard inspection included in the part price and lead time. Additional inspections which include detailed reports, such as First Article (FAIR) and CMM inspections, are available. See more on our inspection services page. What are your tolerances for CNC machined parts? +.005”/-.005” local tolerances across most geometries in metals, +/- 0.010" for plastics. Will vary for large parts, specifically when holding flatness over large parts after heat treatment. Finish requirements for “As Milled” finish will have a minimum 125 surface finish for CNC parts. All fabricated parts have a 0.010” dimensional and 1° angular tolerance. Tapped holes not explicitly called out as Features on the quoted CAD model may be machined to the diameters specified in that model. No surface treatments (e.g. anodize, bead blast, iridite, powder coat, etc.) will be applied unless you have paid for them and we have specifically acknowledged them. What are your CNC machining & turning capabilities? Xometry has significant CNC capabilities in machining through our shop services and the Manufacturing Partner Network . In general, here are some guidelines for machine size but if you do have a quote that pushes to RFQ please make sure to request a quote review so we can take a look! ‣ 5 Axis Machining up to 26″ ‣ 4 Axis Machining up to 36″ ‣ 3 Axis Machining up to 60″ ‣ Dual Spindle Lathes with 32″ Swing, 18″ Max Diameter, and 8″ Chuck ‣ Wire EDM with a part depth of 18″ Do you offer Quick-Turn CNC Machining? Yes! Xometry offers fast lead times on quick-turn parts, with many parts available in 3-4 days. We offer an expedite option, and our team works closely with you to meet your most urgent deadlines. Will I need to pay tariffs on internationally produced parts? Xometry's checkout price for internationally produced prototypes shipped to the U.S. includes tariffs and shipping for standard parcels. You can learn more by reading our article on understanding international shipping costs . Advantages and Challenges of CNC Machining Advantages of CNC Machining CNC milling and turning are highly accurate and repeatable processes. Tight tolerances between +/-0.001″ – 0.005″ can be achieved, depending on specifications. Machines can be programmed to reliably run for 24 hours, 7 days a week if necessary, so CNC milling is a good way of getting parts produced on demand. Using standard tooling, a CNC machining service is particularly valuable for creating one-off parts, custom CNC parts, i.e., for replacing legacy components or delivering a specialized upgrade to a customer. It is also conceivable to scale single-part production to runs exceeding 10,000 units. Depending on the unit number, size, and complexity, the turnaround for CNC machined parts can be as short as one day. With shipping and delivery, deadlines can be met within a week. Another primary advantage of CNC technology is its achievable mechanical properties. By cutting away from bulk material, rather than thermally transforming it as in injection-molding or additive manufacturing, all desirable mechanical properties of the metal or plastic of choice are retained. More than 50 industrial-grade metals, alloys, and plastics can be machined using CNC milling and turning. This selection includes aluminum, brass, bronze, titanium, stainless steel, PEEK, ABS, and zinc. The only material requirement for CNC machining is that the part has an adequate hardness to be fixtured and cut. Challenges of CNC Machining One trade-off when taking advantage of the high performance of CNC manufacturing services is that geometric complexity comes at a cost. Simple, chunky parts are the best designs for CNC milling and turning. There will always be some design limitations due to tool access, although the degree of this effect is relative to the number of axes on the machine. In other words, the more axes used, the more complex the features can be achieved. Another trade-off is that start-up CNC machining costs can be expensive. It is necessary to have a trained professional perform the setup, tool loading, and programming on CNC mills and lathes. Luckily this cost is fixed, so by taking advantage of the same setup for multiple parts, it becomes more economical. Saving money is also achieved by keeping part repositioning to a minimum. Zinc Plating Provides uniform zinc coating which offers protection from corrosion, oxidation, and wear on irregular surfaces. Conforms to ASTM B633-15. What is CNC Machining? CNC, or computer numerical control machining, is a widely used manufacturing process that uses automated, high-speed cutting tools to form designs from metal or plastic stock. Standard CNC machines include 3-axis, 4-axis, and 5-axis milling machines, lathes, and routers. Machines may vary in how CNC machined parts are cut—the workpiece may remain in place while the tool moves, the tool may remain in place while the workpiece is rotated and moved, or both the cutting tool and workpiece may move together. Skilled machinists operate a CNC machine by programming tool paths based on the geometry of the final machined parts. The part geometry information is provided by a CAD (computer-aided design) model. CNC machines can cut almost any metal alloy and rigid plastic with high precision and repeatability, making custom CNC machined parts suitable for nearly every industry, including aerospace , medical, robotics, electronics, and industrial . Xometry provides CNC services and offers custom CNC quotes on over 40 materials ranging from commodity aluminum and acetal to advanced titanium and engineered plastics like PEEK and Teflon. Get More Tips With Our Complete Design Guide Download CNC Guide CNC Machining FAQs How does CNC machining work? CNC machining uses subtractive processes , which means feedstock is machined to its final form by subtracting and removing material. Holes are drilled, lots and pathways are bored, and metal stock is shaped into new material with varying tapers, diameters, and shapes. For subtractive manufacturing, shapes are achieved by the subtraction of material. This contrasts with other types such as additive manufacturing — where materials are added, layered, and deformed to a specified shape. It also contrasts with injection molding where the material is injected in a different state of matter, using a mold, and formed to a specified shape. CNC machining is versatile — and can be used with various materials , including metals, plastics, wood, glass, foam, and other composite materials. This versatility has helped make CNC machining a popular choice across industries , enabling designers and engineers to fabricate products efficiently and precisely. How does CNC machining differ from traditional machining? In traditional machining, a skilled machinist operates a machine, removing or forming metal. This is done according to specifications provided by designers and engineers, usually through an engineering drawing or blueprint. They use turn wheels, dials, switches, chucks, vices, and a variety of cutting tools made of hardened steel, carbide, and industrial diamond, then use measurement instruments to ensure all of the dimensions are correct. CNC machining performs the same function as traditional machining — metal cutting, drilling, milling, boring, grinding, and other metal forming and removal functions — but CNC machines use computer numerical control rather than manual control by a machinist. It is automated, driven by code, and developed by programmers. It is about as precise the first time of cutting as the 500th. Widely used in digital manufacturing (and sometimes in low-volume production runs), it can be revised and altered for modifications and different materials . This type of machining is much more precise and has superseded traditional machining (though not entirely) in manufacturing, fabrication, and industrial production. It uses mathematical coordinates and computing power to achieve the same end with the greatest accuracy. Specifically, computer numerical control uses Cartesian coordinates. These are spatial coordinates — in several dimensions — using coordinates and axes. The automation of cutting tool machines controls its cutting, boring, drilling, or other operation using the numerical control of a computer that reads the coordinates. These coordinates were designated by engineers in the product’s digital drawing and design. What industries use CNC machining? CNC machining is widely used across industries. It is common in aerospace, automotive , consumer electronics, robotics, agriculture, and other fields that frequently use metal parts. It is also widely used in medical devices , household goods, energy, oil and gas , and other consumer applications. It is one of the most common manufacturing processes in the world. What is the history of CNC machining? During World War II, the United States was quickly churning out ships, aircraft, and vehicles for the military. And even once the war ended, production kept up as the country experienced a post-war boom in home construction, infrastructure expansion, and transportation. Naturally, engineers and designers needed tools to help them efficiently meet the growing demand for industrial products. Enter CNC machining . John T. Parsons, who worked in the production of helicopter rotor blades, was one of the first people to champion CNC machining. He and his colleagues at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio used interpolation curves, which could be applied to machining with computational methods, to achieve the complex tapers required for rotor blades. As Parsons’ company got called upon to make more and more complex aircraft parts, they turned to computational methods and cnc machined parts to achieve their desired shapes. This was partly the genesis of CNC machining. Building off of Parsons’ innovations, MIT’s Servomechanisms Laboratory later developed a working machine able to use computational methods to fabricate precise machine parts. Their servo-mechanisms were able to use the Cartesian coordinates — the numerical control — to steer the machine and its moving parts, to fabricate with automated precision. Such automation only grew more sophisticated through the rest of the twentieth century and continues to develop today. What are your inspection options for CNC machining? All machined and sheet metal parts will receive a standard inspection included in the part price and lead time. Additional inspections which include detailed reports, such as First Article (FAIR) and CMM inspections, are available. See more on our inspection services page. What are your tolerances for CNC machined parts? +.005”/-.005” local tolerances across most geometries in metals, +/- 0.010" for plastics. Will vary for large parts, specifically when holding flatness over large parts after heat treatment. Finish requirements for “As Milled” finish will have a minimum 125 surface finish for CNC parts. All fabricated parts have a 0.010” dimensional and 1° angular tolerance. Tapped holes not explicitly called out as Features on the quoted CAD model may be machined to the diameters specified in that model. No surface treatments (e.g. anodize, bead blast, iridite, powder coat, etc.) will be applied unless you have paid for them and we have specifically acknowledged them. What are your CNC machining & turning capabilities? Xometry has significant CNC capabilities in machining through our shop services and the Manufacturing Partner Network . In general, here are some guidelines for machine size but if you do have a quote that pushes to RFQ please make sure to request a quote review so we can take a look! ‣ 5 Axis Machining up to 26″ ‣ 4 Axis Machining up to 36″ ‣ 3 Axis Machining up to 60″ ‣ Dual Spindle Lathes with 32″ Swing, 18″ Max Diameter, and 8″ Chuck ‣ Wire EDM with a part depth of 18″ Do you offer Quick-Turn CNC Machining? Yes! Xometry offers fast lead times on quick-turn parts, with many parts available in 3-4 days. We offer an expedite option, and our team works closely with you to meet your most urgent deadlines. Will I need to pay tariffs on internationally produced parts? Xometry's checkout price for internationally produced prototypes shipped to the U.S. includes tariffs and shipping for standard parcels. You can learn more by reading our article on understanding international shipping costs . Advantages and Challenges of CNC Machining Advantages of CNC Machining CNC milling and turning are highly accurate and repeatable processes. Tight tolerances between +/-0.001″ – 0.005″ can be achieved, depending on specifications. Machines can be programmed to reliably run for 24 hours, 7 days a week if necessary, so CNC milling is a good way of getting parts produced on demand. Using standard tooling, a CNC machining service is particularly valuable for creating one-off parts, custom CNC parts, i.e., for replacing legacy components or delivering a specialized upgrade to a customer. It is also conceivable to scale single-part production to runs exceeding 10,000 units. Depending on the unit number, size, and complexity, the turnaround for CNC machined parts can be as short as one day. With shipping and delivery, deadlines can be met within a week. Another primary advantage of CNC technology is its achievable mechanical properties. By cutting away from bulk material, rather than thermally transforming it as in injection-molding or additive manufacturing, all desirable mechanical properties of the metal or plastic of choice are retained. More than 50 industrial-grade metals, alloys, and plastics can be machined using CNC milling and turning. This selection includes aluminum, brass, bronze, titanium, stainless steel, PEEK, ABS, and zinc. The only material requirement for CNC machining is that the part has an adequate hardness to be fixtured and cut. Challenges of CNC Machining One trade-off when taking advantage of the high performance of CNC manufacturing services is that geometric complexity comes at a cost. Simple, chunky parts are the best designs for CNC milling and turning. There will always be some design limitations due to tool access, although the degree of this effect is relative to the number of axes on the machine. In other words, the more axes used, the more complex the features can be achieved. Another trade-off is that start-up CNC machining costs can be expensive. It is necessary to have a trained professional perform the setup, tool loading, and programming on CNC mills and lathes. Luckily this cost is fixed, so by taking advantage of the same setup for multiple parts, it becomes more economical. Saving money is also achieved by keeping part repositioning to a minimum. Machining at 5-axis and above can sometimes be more economical on multi-faceted geometries because it eliminates the need to manually reposition the part. The wire EDM method of machining can be slow and expensive relative to other processes, and the range of materials that can be used is shortened as they must be electrically conductive. Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport.
